title: Reconfigurable bus-based quantum router for modular superconducting processors
authors: Benzheng Yuan, chaojie Zhang, Yangyang Fei, Chuanbing Han, Haoran He, Huihui Sun, Bo Zhao, Fudong Liu, Weilong Wang, Zheng Shan
abstract: Scaling superconducting quantum processors requires interconnects that provide both non-local connectivity and parallel entangling operations. Nearest-neighbour couplings require distant interactions to be routed through SWAP networks, increasing the native two-qubit-gate count and potentially extending the circuit critical path. Here we introduce a bus-based reconfigurable quantum router for modular superconducting processors. Flux-tunable SQUID couplers selectively connect interface qubits to two shared buses, allowing destructive interference to suppress idle interactions while supporting two disjoint controlled-$Z$ (CZ) gates in parallel. Full-system Hamiltonian simulations yield parallel-gate errors at the level of $10^{-3}$, and open-system analysis identifies the coherence requirements for high-fidelity operation. We further assess the circuit-level consequences using hardware-aware compilation and resource-constrained scheduling. For 36-qubit quantum Fourier transform (QFT), QAOA-MaxCut and random-pairing circuits, the router reduces the median SWAP count by up to $34\%$ and the native CZ count by up to $20\%$ relative to a matched two-dimensional grid. End-to-end depth reduction is circuit dependent, reaching $20\%$ for QAOA-MaxCut but remaining negligible for the QFT despite its lower gate count. These results show that enhanced connectivity and schedulable parallelism provide distinct benefits, establishing the router as a compiler-visible hardware resource for modular superconducting quantum processors.
summary: This paper introduces a novel bus-based reconfigurable quantum router designed for modular superconducting quantum processors to overcome limitations in connectivity. By using flux-tunable SQUID couplers, the router enables parallel two-qubit gates and significantly reduces the required number of SWAP and CZ gates for complex circuits. The results establish the router as a critical, compiler-visible hardware resource for scaling quantum computation.
main_problem: Scaling superconducting quantum processors requires interconnects that provide non-local connectivity and parallel entangling operations, as nearest-neighbor couplings necessitate SWAP networks.
main_result: The proposed bus-based router reduces the median SWAP count by up to 34% and the native CZ count by up to 20% compared to a 2D grid, demonstrating that enhanced connectivity and schedulable parallelism provide distinct benefits.
method: The authors used full-system Hamiltonian simulations, open-system analysis, and hardware-aware compilation to evaluate the router's performance on various quantum circuits.
model_or_system: The system is a superconducting quantum processor featuring a bus-based reconfigurable quantum router. It uses flux-tunable SQUID couplers to selectively connect interface qubits to two shared buses (Lane A and Lane B).
key_observables: Gate error ($\sim 10^{-3}$ for parallel gates), reduction in SWAP count (up to 34%), reduction in CZ count (up to 20%), and circuit depth reduction (up to 20% for QAOA-MaxCut).
important_parameters: The system relies on operating in a bufferless regime and requires dynamic, real-time hardware control.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the ability to selectively suppress idle interactions via destructive interference and that the router can be integrated into a compiler-visible resource model.
figures_summary: The figures conceptually illustrate the router's schematic, the equivalent cQED circuit model, and the physical flip-chip layout connecting peripheral computational modules to the central router layer.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying the scaling bottleneck (SWAP networks) to proposing the physical architecture (SQUID-coupled buses), detailing the Hamiltonian and coupling mechanisms, and finally benchmarking the resource reduction benefits across specific quantum algorithms (QFT, QAOA-MaxCut).
why_interesting: The work directly addresses the physical implementation challenges of scaling quantum processors by providing a hardware-level solution for interconnectivity and parallel gate scheduling, which is crucial for realizing large-scale quantum computation.
